CV: CARDS and EEHPC Labs, UMBC, Research Assistant, Autonomous Vehicles, October 2021 - September 2022.
CV: streamed the Crazyflie AI-deck camera into NumPy matrices over sockets for YOLO/OpenCV object detection, letting several autonomous-navigation teams progress regardless of graphics platform.

David (2026-11-04) / KB / page: two detectors ran in parallel. Onboard: an obstacle-detection network on the drone plus a flight state machine David coded, driven by the drone's sensors (obstacle detection and wall following). Ground station: YOLO object detection through OpenCV for target tracking, fed by a streamer David wrote by hand: the AI-deck streams camera frames over its ESP32 WiFi, and his code pulls in the raw bits over sockets and decodes them into NumPy frames (public repo CF2-Computervision). YOLO did NOT run on the drone. Uses: target tracking and building mapping. The streamer was lightweight enough for a higher frame rate and annotated the live view with each object or obstacle the Crazyflie detected.
CV/KB: cut swarm reaction time 40% with a C/C++ state machine; built odometry-based maps of flight trajectories.
CV/KB: wrote C programs and RISC-V firmware for the GAP8 on the AI-deck (GreenWaves PMSIS SDK: dispatching work across its 8-core cluster, UART, status LED).
KB: when stacked decks used up the Crazyflie's UART ports, David carried the GAP8-to-STM32 link over the deck's I2C lines as a clocked, SPI-style protocol.
KB/README: the original firmware was not recovered; the link was re-created in November 2026 and verified in a logic-level simulation only (public repo aideck-bitbang-link), not on hardware.

KB/README: SCL is the clock and SDA the data; SDA changes only while SCL is low, so the protocol never forms an I2C START and the EEPROM and sensor decks on the bus ignore it; each frame ends with a deliberate I2C STOP, which resets bystanders and clears the STM32 I2C BUSY flag.

Sim results (aideck-bitbang-link out/results.json, portfolio page): 200 of 200 frames byte-exact at 250 kHz, checked by the STM32-side receiver, a separate Python decoder and sigrok; 0 STARTs; 20,000-frame fault run: 8,036 corrupted frames all rejected, 0 false accepts, 11,964 clean frames delivered, recovered after all 1,011 garbage bursts; clean up to 500 kHz with typical interrupt latency and 100 kHz allowing rare 5 microsecond stalls (1.5 MHz with no latency).
Sim assumptions: 300 ns line rise time and modeled interrupt latency; frames are 17 bytes (sync word, length, 12-byte YOLO-style detection record, CRC-16).

Portfolio page/datasheets: Crazyflie 2.1 has an STM32F405 (Cortex-M4, 168 MHz) and an nRF51822 radio/power MCU; AI-deck has a GAP8 (8+1 RISC-V cores), HM01B0 320x320 camera, NINA-W102 ESP32 WiFi, HyperFlash and HyperRAM. GAP8 UART goes to the Crazyflie's UART1; the ESP32 to UART2; Lighthouse and Loco decks also use UART1; AI-deck errata: GAP8 UART TX does not work while HyperFlash is in use.
CV: poster 'Energy-Efficient Onboard Autonomous Drone Navigation: Wall Following and Obstacle Detection', URCAD 2022, UMBC.

CV: streamed the Crazyflie AI-deck camera into NumPy matrices over sockets for YOLO/OpenCV object detection, letting several autonomous-navigation teams progress regardless of graphics platform.

David (2026-11-04) / KB / page: two detectors ran in parallel. Onboard: an obstacle-detection network on the drone plus a flight state machine David coded, driven by the drone's sensors (obstacle detection and wall following). Ground station: YOLO object detection through OpenCV for target tracking, fed by a streamer David wrote by hand: the AI-deck streams camera frames over its ESP32 WiFi, and his code pulls in the raw bits over sockets and decodes them into NumPy frames (public repo CF2-Computervision). YOLO did NOT run on the drone. Uses: target tracking and building mapping. The streamer was lightweight enough for a higher frame rate and annotated the live view with each object or obstacle the Crazyflie detected.
CV/KB: cut swarm reaction time 40% with a C/C++ state machine; built odometry-based maps of flight trajectories.
CV/KB: wrote C programs and RISC-V firmware for the GAP8 on the AI-deck (GreenWaves PMSIS SDK: dispatching work across its 8-core cluster, UART, status LED).
KB: when stacked decks used up the Crazyflie's UART ports, David carried the GAP8-to-STM32 link over the deck's I2C lines as a clocked, SPI-style protocol.
KB/README: the original firmware was not recovered; the link was re-created in November 2026 and verified in a logic-level simulation only (public repo aideck-bitbang-link), not on hardware.

David (2026-11-04) / KB / page: two detectors ran in parallel. Onboard: an obstacle-detection network on the drone plus a flight state machine David coded, driven by the drone's sensors (obstacle detection and wall following). Ground station: YOLO object detection through OpenCV for target tracking, fed by a streamer David wrote by hand: the AI-deck streams camera frames over its ESP32 WiFi, and his code pulls in the raw bits over sockets and decodes them into NumPy frames (public repo CF2-Computervision). YOLO did NOT run on the drone. Uses: target tracking and building mapping. The streamer was lightweight enough for a higher frame rate and annotated the live view with each object or obstacle the Crazyflie detected.
CV/KB: cut swarm reaction time 40% with a C/C++ state machine; built odometry-based maps of flight trajectories.
CV/KB: wrote C programs and RISC-V firmware for the GAP8 on the AI-deck (GreenWaves PMSIS SDK: dispatching work across its 8-core cluster, UART, status LED).
KB: when stacked decks used up the Crazyflie's UART ports, David carried the GAP8-to-STM32 link over the deck's I2C lines as a clocked, SPI-style protocol.
KB/README: the original firmware was not recovered; the link was re-created in November 2026 and verified in a logic-level simulation only (public repo aideck-bitbang-link), not on hardware.

KB/README: SCL is the clock and SDA the data; SDA changes only while SCL is low, so the protocol never forms an I2C START and the EEPROM and sensor decks on the bus ignore it; each frame ends with a deliberate I2C STOP, which resets bystanders and clears the STM32 I2C BUSY flag.

Sim results (aideck-bitbang-link out/results.json, portfolio page): 200 of 200 frames byte-exact at 250 kHz, checked by the STM32-side receiver, a separate Python decoder and sigrok; 0 STARTs; 20,000-frame fault run: 8,036 corrupted frames all rejected, 0 false accepts, 11,964 clean frames delivered, recovered after all 1,011 garbage bursts; clean up to 500 kHz with typical interrupt latency and 100 kHz allowing rare 5 microsecond stalls (1.5 MHz with no latency).
Sim assumptions: 300 ns line rise time and modeled interrupt latency; frames are 17 bytes (sync word, length, 12-byte YOLO-style detection record, CRC-16).

GAP8 UART goes to the Crazyflie's UART1; the ESP32 to UART2; Lighthouse and Loco decks also use UART1; AI-deck errata: GAP8 UART TX does not work while HyperFlash is in use.
